list.listitem: Suspect dermatitis herpetiformis (DH) in patients presenting with pruritic grouped papulovesicles distributed symmetrically in classical extensor areas, buttocks, back, or scalp. C

After an initial lesional biopsy demonstrating histopathologic findings suggestive of DH, establish a definitive diagnosis using direct immunofluorescence (DIF) microscopy of perilesional skin. Order serologic markers if DIF cannot be performed or is inconclusive. C

A gluten-free diet (GFD) may provide long-term control of underlying gluten sensitivity, protection against DH relapses, and may decrease the risk of developing gastric lymphoma. Perform diagnostic testing prior to starting GFD. C

Consider dapsone therapy in patients with severe DH, GFD-refractory DH, or patients unwilling or unable to adhere to GFD. Low dose therapy starts at 25 mg daily to twice daily, increased by 25 mg/day every week until disease control is achieved, with a maximum daily dose of 200 mg. C

background.definition: Dermatitis herpetiformis is an intensely pruritic polymorphic papulovesicular eruption associated with underlying celiac disease (CD), primarily affecting the extensor surfaces of elbows and knees, buttocks, back, and scalp. It is one of four major groups of autoimmune blistering diseases (AIBDs); the other three being pemphigus, pemphigoid, and epidermolysis bullosa acquisita.

list.listitem: Incidence ranges from 0.9 to 2.6 per 100,000 per year. Patients of Northern European descent are most commonly affected.
Prevalence ranges from 1.2 to 39.2 per 100,000.
Five percent to 25% of patients with celiac disease present with DH; most DH patients do not have symptomatic CD, but more than 90% demonstrate CD-associated changes upon endoscopy.
DH has a statistically significant association with lymphoma, most often of the non-Hodgkin’s type but also Hodgkin’s lymphoma and B-cell lymphoma.

There have also been reports of DH being associated with carcinoma of the lung, prostate, breast, skin, thyroid, pancreas, stomach, colon, and rectum. DH has also been associated with autoimmune conditions, including autoimmune induced hypothyroidism due to Hashimoto's thyroiditis, insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus, pernicious anemia, Addison's disease, alopecia areata, myasthenia gravis, systemic lupus erythematosus, and vitiligo.
Immune-mediated disorder triggered by gluten (gliadin peptides), associated mainly with human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8.
Less common triggers include gastric surgery, iodine containing products, and leuprolide acetate.
DH is one part of a spectrum of gluten-sensitivity disorders that include CD and IgA nephropathy. Patients often have a genetic predisposition to development of gluten sensitivity.
IgA antibodies are formed to gluten-transglutaminase complexes and deposit in the papillary dermis.
IgA deposition leads to neutrophilic infiltrate, activation of the complement cascade, and subsequent cutaneous lesions.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: First-degree relative with DH or CD
Northern European ancestry (rare in Asians and Africans)

list.listitem: Suspect DH in patients presenting with pruritic grouped papulovesicles distributed symmetrically in classical extensor areas. C

After performing a 4mm punch biopsy of a primary lesion demonstrating histopathologic findings suggestive of DH, confirm the diagnosis using DIF microscopy of perilesional skin revealing microgranular IgA deposits at the dermal papillae and the dermal-epidermal junction. C

If DIF cannot be performed or is inconclusive, consider performing a serologic test using either indirect immunofluorescence (IIF) microscopy for endomysial antibodies (EMA) or transglutaminase isoenzyme 2 (TG2) immunoassay. The latter can also be used to verify dietary adherence during follow-up. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Bullae are larger than the DH vesicles and usually scattered.
Oral and mucous membrane involvement is much more likely.
Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgA deposits as opposed to granular.
Lesions are primarily on the trunk with histopathologic acantholysis.
Primary lesions are wheals and are not confined to specific distributions.
Cutaneous findings are usually minimal, and burrows may be present.
Presentation depends on subtype, but the combination of lesions and distribution is unlikely to resemble DH.

list.listitem: Suspect DH in patients presenting with pruritic grouped papulovesicles distributed symmetrically in classical extensor areas. Approximately 15% to 20% of patients will have a history of CD or symptoms consistent with it.

Primary lesions are grouped erythematous papules or vesicles, often herpetiform. Patients may present with only erosions and excoriations secondary to scratching in the classic cutaneous distribution.

Patients complain of intense pruritus or burning, which may precede cutaneous findings. Classically, rash is distributed symmetrically on the extensor surfaces of the elbows and knees as well as the buttocks, back, and scalp. Lesions are rarely present on the face and groin.
Acral petechiae and purpura (of the fingers and toes) are common but may be hard to appreciate, hence dermoscopy may be useful for these areas.
Rash is intermittent and may worsen with dietary intake of gluten. Lesions may heal without scarring, but post-inflammatory dyspigmentation may occur.
Patients with darker skin phototypes typically present with cutaneous findings similar to those with fair skin.
Oral mucosal involvement in the form of erythematous, vesicular, purpuric, or erosive lesions is rare.

A definitive diagnosis of DH requires two skin biopsies. Histopathology of initial 4mm punch biopsy of primary lesion (transported via formalin container) typically reveals neutrophilic microabscesses in the dermal papillae for papules and subepidermal blistering for vesicles. Neutrophilic microabscesses may be seen in other bullous conditions and, hence, are not entirely specific for DH.

DIF microscopy of perilesional biopsy (obtained with a 4mm punch biopsy and transported in a non-formalin transport medium) is the gold standard for diagnosis of DH and reveals granular IgA deposits along the tips of the dermal papillae and at the dermo-epidermal junction. DIF microscopy has a 92.4% sensitivity.

Serum antibodies present in patients with DH should not be used for definitive diagnosis but may be useful adjuncts. If DIF cannot be performed or is inconclusive, consider performing a serologic test using either indirect immunofluorescence (IIF) microscopy for endomysial antibodies (EMA) or transglutaminase isoenzyme 2 (TG2) immunoassay. IIF for EMA is 90% sensitive and 96% specific for diagnosis of DH. TG antibodies are 89% sensitive and 98% specific for DH (LR+ 44, LR- 0.11).

Testing for associated disease may include thyroid function testing, fasting blood glucose, anti-thyroid peroxidase testing, and testing for other autoimmune diseases if indicated by history and physical.
Suspect DH in patients with papulovesicles along extensor areas and/or pre-existing CD.

Definitive diagnosis requires skin biopsy with DIF staining for IgA. One biopsy should be taken from a primary lesion for routine histology and another biopsy performed on perilesional (normal) skin for DIF microscopy.
The presence of anti-EMA is highly specific for underlying gluten-sensitive enteropathy and should be ordered to rule out the disease. Anti-tTG testing is an alternative.
See Figure 1 in chapter on celiac disease for the approach to diagnosis of that condition.

Institution of a (GFD) provides long-term control of underlying gluten sensitivity, protection against DH relapses, and may afford protection against GI lymphoma. It is crucial to perform all diagnostic testing prior to starting GFD to minimize false negative results. C

Consider dapsone therapy in patients with severe DH, GFD-refractory DH, or patients unwilling or unable to adhere to GFD. Starting dose is 25 mg daily to twice daily, increased by 25 mg/day every week until disease control is achieved, with a maximum daily dose of 200 mg. Resolution of symptoms could occur as quickly as 3 to 4 days. C

Dapsone is the most widely used treatment and is recommended for patients with severe DH, GFD-refractory DH, or patients unwilling or unable to adhere to a gluten-free diet (GFD). It has a dramatic effect on the rash, clearing it up within 3 to 4 days. Low dose therapy starts at 25 mg daily to twice daily, increased by 25 mg/day every week until disease control is achieved, with a maximum daily dose of 200 mg. High dose therapy for patients with severe cutaneous manifestations starts at 50mg twice to three times daily in patients without glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PDH) deficiency.
Evaluate serum G6PDH activity prior to initiating dapsone therapy. This guides the choice between low and high dose therapy, especially in severe cases.
The main side effects of dapsone are methemoglobinemia, hemolysis, and fatal agranulocytosis. They are related to the toxic metabolite hydroxylamine produced by cytochrome P-450.

At baseline, obtain CBC with differential and reticulocyte count, liver and renal function panels, and serum G6PD level. Repeat CBC, reticulocyte count, and methemoglobin level (if dapsone dose >150 mg daily) every week during the first month of treatment, then every 2 weeks for the second and third months. Monitor liver and renal function panels every 2 weeks during the first three months of dapsone therapy. Thereafter, check CBC, reticulocyte count, methemoglobin level (if dapsone dose >150 mg daily), liver and renal function panels every 3 months.
Hypersensitivity syndrome with resultant hypothyroidism may occur with dapsone therapy, hence consider thyroid function testing for symptomatic patients.

In patients with contraindications to or refractory to dapsone therapy, sulfones such as sulfasalazine, sulfamethoxypyridazine, and sulfapyridine may be considered. Evidence is mostly from uncontrolled trials and observational studies. Sulfones are generally less effective than dapsone for DH.
Potent topical corticosteroids and oral antihistamines may be considered for symptomatic treatment of DH.
Weak evidence supports the use of tetracycline plus nicotinamide as well as colchicine as alternative therapies for DH.
Anecdotal data suggest that rituximab may be an alternative treatment for DH.

A consensus statement for the diagnosis and treatment of DH from the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology discourages the use of cyclosporine given the dangerous range of published dosage. It also found concluded that systemic glucocorticoids ineffective.

A gluten-free diet (GFD) effectively targets the underlying cause of DH, which is related to proteins in wheat, barley, rye, and oats. Diet therapy alone results in clearing of the lesions after 6 to 24 months.
A GFD is essential to maintain a relapse-free state if dapsone therapy is not used long-term.
It is crucial to perform all diagnostic testing prior to starting GFD to minimize false negative results.
TG2-based immunoassay (ELISA) may be used to monitor GFD adherence during follow-up.
Refer patients to a dietician for counseling on the maintenance of a GFD.

Referral to a gastroenterologist is advised for patients with significant GI symptoms including malabsorption. Small bowel endoscopy with biopsy, especially of the duodenum, is recommended to evaluate the severity of enteropathy.
Although untreated CD may result in a higher incidence of non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma, the long-term mortality rate in patients with DH remains even lower than that of the general population. B

A meta-analysis of 52 studies with 30 different autoimmune conditions, showed association of gastric carcinoma with pooled autoimmune conditions (RR 1.37; 95% CI, 1.24 to 1.52) and association with DH (RR 1.74; 95% CI 1.02-2.97 n = 3 studies). B

9.5% of DH patients have associated systemic disorders: 4.3% autoimmune thyroid diseases, 1.0% insulin-dependent diabetes, 1.3% lupus erythematous, 1.0% Sjögren's syndrome, 1.3% sarcoidosis, and 1.6% vitiligo or alopecia areata. C
In patients older than 50 years, consider evaluation for coexistent malignancy.

Sulfamethoxypyridazine may be useful for the treatment of patients older than 50 years. The dose ranges from 0.5 g twice a week to 4.0 g daily. Side effects include nausea, lethargy, depression, bone marrow depression, and hemolytic anemia.
